perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I acted in ways that go against who I am
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for this trauma profile. As a male firefighter whose index trauma is relief work in a war zone, moral-violation cues are plausible, but 'Babies' and especially 'Comments on sexual violence' imply highly specific trauma-linked content that is not supported anywhere else in the memory, threat, or appraisal items. Those other nodes describe moral injury, disorganized trauma memory, pain recall, anger, and global alienation, but contain no infant-related or sexual-violence-related material. This makes those two triggers feel disconnected from the rest of the formulation rather than part of the same trauma network.

issues.explanation: Within Maladaptive Strategies, 'Avoid Feelings' is internally contradictory in wording: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of emotional avoidance. It conflicts with the node label and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise suggests suppression/avoidance and control strategies in response to distress. This item is therefore not clinically coherent as selected.

issues.item: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: This item directly contradicts the Maladaptive Strategies construct and the rest of the profile. 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes openness to emotion rather than avoidance of feelings. It is internally inconsistent within the node, where the other items are clearly maladaptive avoidance/control strategies (self-harm to regulate affect, mental rituals to prevent recurrence), and it does not fit the cognitive formulation linking negative appraisals, memory, and threat to maladaptive coping.

vignette: Kiet had always been drawn to helping others, which is why he became a firefighter and later volunteered to work in war zones as a relief worker. It was on one of these missions that his life changed forever. He remembers the sound of explosions and gunfire, the smell of smoke and sweat, and the sight of innocent civilians caught in the crossfire. But it's not just the chaos of the scene that haunts him - it's what happened next. As Kiet was trying to assist a young girl who had been injured, he saw one of his fellow relief workers take advantage of her, sexually assaulting her while she lay helpless on the ground. The image is seared into Kiet's mind, and even now, years later, he can't shake the feeling of guilt and shame that he didn't act sooner to stop it. Since then, certain sounds - like explosions or bangs - send Kiet's heart racing and transport him back to that moment. He becomes irritable and withdrawn, lashing out at those around him for no reason. Even when there is unusual silence, Kiet feels a sense of unease, as if something dangerous is lurking just beneath the surface. Kiet has tried various ways to cope with his emotions, but they often backfire. When he's feeling overwhelmed, he turns to self-harm - physically hurting himself as a way to release the pent-up feelings. He also performs mental rituals, trying to convince himself that if he just does things in a certain order or repeats specific phrases, he can prevent bad things from happening again. But these strategies only provide temporary relief. The memories of what happened continue to haunt him, and Kiet often finds himself reliving the physical pain of that day - the ache in his muscles, the tightness in his chest. He tries to push the thoughts away, but they linger just beneath the surface, waiting to pounce. Kiet's struggles have taken a toll on his personal life. His divorce was partly due to his inability to connect with his wife, who couldn't understand why he was so withdrawn and angry all the time. Even now, Kiet feels like he doesn't belong anywhere - not at home, not at work, not in his own skin. As a firefighter, Kiet is constantly surrounded by triggers - the sounds of sirens, the smell of smoke, the sight of people in distress. He tries to avoid certain calls or situations that might remind him too much of what happened, but it's getting harder and harder to keep up the charade. His colleagues have started to notice his withdrawal, and Kiet fears that if he doesn't get help soon, he'll lose everything - his job, his friends, himself. It was a particularly rough call last week that finally pushed Kiet to seek help. He was responding to a domestic violence incident, and the sound of the woman's screams transported him right back to that war zone. For the first time in years, Kiet felt like he couldn't breathe - like he was drowning under the weight of his own memories. As he sits in the therapist's office now, Kiet is both scared and hopeful. He knows it won't be easy, but for the first time in a long time, he feels like there might be a way out - a way to confront his demons, to find some measure of peace, and to learn how to live with himself again.
